hook: Uber Will Now Drive Your *10-Year-Old* Solo
dek: Uber Kids lets 10-year-olds ride alone in 3 cities, with drivers paid extra to do it.

slides.label: What happened
slides.text: Uber quietly launched *Uber Kids*, a pilot letting children as young as 10 ride without an adult.

slides.label: Where
slides.text: It's running in *Austin, Nashville,* and *Madison*, building on Uber's existing teen ride service for ages 13 to 17.

slides.label: Parent rules
slides.text: Parents must add their child to a family profile, finish safety onboarding, and *be at pickup* in person.

slides.label: Driver rules
slides.text: Only invited, highly rated drivers qualify, and they must complete a training module before joining.

slides.label: Safety tech
slides.text: Every ride needs *PIN verification*, encrypted live video, plus GPS sensors that flag detours or sudden stops.

slides.label: The pay
slides.text: Qualifying drivers earn *$7 extra* per Uber Kids trip, plus a *$20 bonus* for their first completed ride.

slides.label: Status
slides.text: Uber calls it a *limited pilot* that could expand nationwide, or disappear completely by next year.

slides.label: Why it matters
slides.text: Gig drivers, many of them Black and Brown workers, get paid more for added responsibility, while families get a new option.

caption_instagram:
Uber Kids is here, and it means children as young as 10 can now ride Uber alone, no adult required, in a new pilot running in Austin, Nashville, and Madison. It builds on Uber's existing teen ride service for ages 13 to 17.

Parents have to set it up first: adding their kid to a family profile, finishing safety onboarding, and physically being there when the ride starts. Drivers must be invited, highly rated, and trained, and they live-stream the ride so parents can watch. Every trip needs a PIN, GPS tracks the route, and drivers earn $7 extra per ride plus a $20 bonus their first time, according to TechCrunch.

This could reshape pickup lines everywhere, or it could vanish by next year since Uber calls it a limited test. For gig drivers, many of them Black and Brown workers, that extra pay for extra responsibility is worth watching.

caption_linkedin:
Uber is testing a new customer segment: families with young kids. Its new Uber Kids pilot lets children as young as 10 ride alone in Austin, Nashville, and Madison, building on the existing Uber for Teens service for ages 13 to 17.

The build is instructive for anyone working on trust and safety products. Parents must onboard through a dedicated profile and be physically present at pickup. Drivers must be invited, highly rated, and trained, then opt into live video streaming so parents can monitor the ride. Every trip requires PIN verification, and GPS sensors flag unexpected stops or route changes.

Uber is also solving a labor problem: drivers get $7 extra per Uber Kids trip and a $20 bonus for their first one, a clear signal that added responsibility needs added pay, something gig platforms built on underrepresented workers rarely price in well.

Uber, per TechCrunch, calls this a limited pilot that may never scale. Still, it's a clean case study in layering safety, incentives, and trust to open a new market.
